headline: Two ★ today, both on learning dynamics he can use for the tree paper: a proof that jointly trained input/output embeddings with d much smaller than V reach near-optimal next-token prediction (one-token context), and a study showing grammar sparsity sets whether transformers learn a random hierarchical language level by level (t ∝ V, then V^3) or all at once (t ∝ √V). Also worth a skim: a replica theory of linear classification on tree-broadcast data, and Yarotsky et al. reducing small-init tensor gradient flow to greedy matching.

daily_picks.title: Can pretrained Transformers deliver semiparametrically efficient inference?
daily_picks.digest:
Setting and problem 
 The semiparametric model. An observation $Z \in \mathcal{Z} \subset \mathbb{R}^{d_z}$ is drawn from an unknown distribution $P$ in a statistical model $\mathcal{P}$. The object of inference is not one functional but a whole query-indexed family
$$\{\beta_q(P) : q \in \mathcal{Q},\ P \in \mathcal{P}\}, \qquad q = (k,u),\ \beta_q(P) \in \mathbb{R}^{d_k},$$
where $k \in \mathcal{K}$ picks an estimand class (ATE, quantile treatment effect, partially linear projection coefficient, mean survival time, group treatment effects, ...) and $u \in \mathcal{U}_k$ is an optional argument (for the QTE, the quantile level $u \in (0,1)$). Everything else about $P$ (outcome regressions $m_d(x) = \mathbb{E}_P(Y \mid D=d, X=x)$, propensity scores, conditional densities, censoring laws) is nuisance. The model $\mathcal{P}$ is essentially nonparametric: all distributions whose density $p = dP/dP_0$ with respect to a fixed reference $P_0$ is bounded between constants $c_0 < p < C_0$. The efficiency bound is
$$V_q^\star(P) = \mathbb{E}_P\{(\psi^\star_{P,q})^{\otimes 2}\},$$

daily_picks.digest:
Setting and problem 
 Object of study. A corpus of long, coherent documents is treated as samples from a stochastic source emitting a symbol sequence $X_1, X_2, \dots, X_T$ (conceptually bytes; operationally tokens of an LLM tokenizer, with all lengths converted back to UTF-8 bytes so that different tokenizers can be compared).  $$h(t, C) = H(X_t \mid X_{t-C}, \dots, X_{t-1}),$$

 Predictive information between adjacent windows. With past $P_C = (X_{t-C+1},\dots,X_t)$ and future $F_C = (X_{t+1},\dots,X_{t+C})$,

researchers.title: Language Model Harnesses can be Compositional Generalizers
researchers.abstract: Modern language models (LMs) are post-trained and deployed as agents inside a "harness", but standard harness designs accumulate context that the neural network is forced to generalize to, making training for long-horizon tasks expensive and time-consuming. We study an alternative emerging path: training inherently neurosymbolic LM harnesses, which externalize and manage context programmatically to compose existing LM capabilities. We hypothesize that training around these harnesses can offer a better return on compute by enabling compositional generalization, as they can learn to decompose complex problems so that every observation their neural LM receives is locally in-distribution, even when the full task is novel. We find that harnesses like the Recursive Language Model (RLM) learn such decompositions readily under reinforcement learning post-training: (1) we demonstrate that training only on short tasks can generalize to tasks 2-64$\times$ longer while the base neural LM improves less, and (2) training on one domain transfers to novel domains that share latent structure. On messier, complex tasks, we find that we can target individual LLM calls within a harness by generating and training on easier, synthetically generated surrogate environments with fake tool / sub-calls, a technique we call surrogate harness training. From this finding, we train RLM-27B on synthetic data, and show it improves Qwen3.8-27B in the same RLM harness on a hard suite of long-context tasks like CTC-Bench and ExpertLongBench by 26.9% on average while using $\sim$2$\times$ fewer tokens at inference time. Finally, we show that harnesses can compose over these newly learned decompositions using recursive sub-harness calls.
researchers.evidence: MIT CSAIL affiliation; co-author Alex L. Zhang (Recursive Language Models)
researchers.summary: Training recursive LM harnesses with RL gives compositional generalization: training on short tasks transfers to 2-64x longer ones; RLM-27B improves long-context suites by 26.9% with ~2x fewer tokens.

researchers.title: PROSPER: LLMs as Sparse Retrievers for First-Stage Product Search
researchers.abstract: Product search is a crucial component of large-scale e-commerce platforms, where first-stage retrieval should achieve high recall while ensuring efficient online deployment. Sparse retrieval remains attractive for this setting due to its interpretability and deployability, yet it suffers from severe vocabulary mismatch challenges, especially for short queries and product titles. Large language models (LLMs) offer strong semantic capabilities, but directly applying them to sparse retrieval in product search introduces new challenges: (i) semantic expansion may distort critical literal signals such as brand names and model identifiers; and (ii) learning meaningful sparse representations is difficult in the high-dimensional vocabulary space induced by LLMs.To address these challenges, we propose PROSPER, a framework that uses LLMs as sparse retrievers for product search while explicitly preserving lexical fidelity. PROSPER combines (i) a literal residual network that alleviates lexical expansion hallucination by reinforcing underweighted literal terms through a residual compensation mechanism; and (ii) a lexical focusing window that uses top-k selection for rapid early sparsification and effective training initialization. Extensive offline evaluations and large-scale online A/B tests demonstrate that PROSPER consistently improves over existing sparse retrievers, and provides revenue gains for industrial hybrid retrieval systems.
researchers.evidence: co-authors Jiafeng Guo, Ruqing Zhang (ICT CAS / UvA collaboration)
researchers.summary: PROSPER: LLM-based learned sparse retrieval for product search (WSDM 2027 oral).

researchers.title: The Temporal Residual: Fast and Effective Retrofitting of Latent Feedback into Pretrained Language Models
researchers.abstract: A transformer language model computes a deep hidden state for every token but uses it only to sample that token. Existing latent-feedback designs, which feed hidden states back across tokens, are mostly built in during pretraining and gain little when added to a pretrained model. We introduce the temporal residual, a second residual stream that every sublayer reads and writes and that is carried from each token to the next. It adds 2,752 parameters to a 4.2B-parameter model and starts exactly at the pretrained network. Retrofitted onto Qwen3.5-4B-Base with 5B tokens of training, it beats a standard model trained on the same data by 7, 13 and 5 points on AIME 2024, AIME 2025 and AMC 2023, writes shorter solutions, and stays ahead at matched training compute. The separate stream matters: prior designs that feed state into the existing stream recover at most 40% of the gain when retrofitted. Validation loss can mislead: the recipe with the lowest loss gains nothing at decoding. Trained with filler tokens in place of reasoning, the model reasons in its hidden state: its GSM8K accuracy with no visible reasoning rises from 21% to 40%, and falls back when the carried state is zeroed.
researchers.summary: A carried 'temporal residual' stream (2,752 extra parameters) retrofitted onto Qwen3.5-4B-Base raises AIME/AMC scores and lets the model reason in hidden state (no-CoT GSM8K 21% → 40%).

researchers.title: Improving semantic equivalence in research-level math formalization
researchers.comments: Accepted at the 6th Math-AI workshop at NeurIPS'26
researchers.abstract: Formalizing mathematics in Lean is never a word-for-word translation of a paper: a Lean formalization changes definitions, strengthens hypotheses, splits arguments, and adds lemmas the paper never mentions. It stands to reason that a model that is good at autoformalization must be a good predictor of how a natural language source must differ from its faithful Lean formalization. With that in mind, we collect 4{,}076 audited examples of such changes from 832 Lean projects that formalize research-level mathematics, and use them to ask a practical question: how well can a model \emph{write} Lean inside a real research-level project that may contain tens of thousands of lines of code, and does training on discrepancies between natural language sources and their faithful Lean formalizations help? Our training set consists of 3{,}431 tasks from 141 repositories, and the test set consists of 645 tasks from the remaining 27 repositories. Training on in-project Lean nearly doubles complete proofs ($11\% \to 20\%$) and raises the share of statements in gold agreement with the project's own formalization by nearly a third ($30\%$ to $39\%$). The gain comes from the pairs themselves: an adapter trained only to predict how the Lean will differ, or a model told the difference in advance, barely helps. Training on where formalizations depart from their sources is thus an effective way of improving semantic equivalence in research-level formalization.
researchers.summary: 4,076 audited NL-vs-Lean discrepancies from 832 research-level Lean projects; training on them improves writing Lean inside real projects (NeurIPS'26 Math-AI workshop).

researchers.title: Does a Frontier Large Language Model Know What It Can Solve? A 100-Conjecture Calibration Study
researchers.comments: Accepted at the 6th AI-Math Workshop at NeurIPS'26
researchers.abstract: How does confidence correlate with actual performance in large language models, when attacking open research-level math problems? We address this question by studying the performance of ChatGPT 5.6 Sol Ultra on a set of 100 open conjectures in geometric analysis. By construction, the model first selected open problems in geometric analysis that it assessed that it had at least a 50\% chance of proving or disproving, and then assigned a probability of success to each question. 13 questions were then excluded after an audit, and the model was asked to resolve the remaining 87 problems. Its mean stated resolution probability was $0.617$, versus an observed rate of $0.103$ (Brier score $0.351$, ECE $0.513$), thereby demonstrating that the model was systematically over-confident in its self-assessment. However, the scores retained ranking signal (AUROC $0.714$). The model was highly overconfident in probability magnitude but did more often than not assign a high probability of success to the problems that it did resolve, than the problems that it did not. Hence, its probabilities were numerically mis-calibrated but directionally correct. All proofs have been formalized in Lean, thereby verifying correctness, and have been run through a semantic equivalence pipeline to ensure semantic equivalence between the formalized and informal statements. These are exploratory campaign outcomes, not fixed-budget success probabilities. The certificates prove formal statements; for a couple of questions, some geometric inputs are assumed in the lean proofs.
researchers.summary: A frontier model's self-assessed success probability on 87 open geometric-analysis conjectures averaged 0.62 vs 0.10 observed: badly overconfident but still rank-informative (AUROC 0.71).

researchers.title: VADE: A Verifiable Agent Data Engine from Professional Sources
researchers.comments: 40 pages, 6 figures, 32 tables. Project page: https://tiger-ai-lab.github.io/VADE/
researchers.abstract: Language agents have shown their practical value, particularly in software engineering, where abundant public code and executable tests support training and evaluation at scale. Extending this success to other professional domains, such as law and finance, is not straightforward: many agent tasks involve open-ended analysis, making outcomes hard to verify and, in turn, hard to use as scalable supervision. As a result, high-quality tasks in these domains are still largely expert-authored, making them expensive to scale and limiting their use for training. To address this bottleneck, we introduce VADE, a data engine that automatically constructs verifiable analysis tasks from public sources used in professional practice. VADE exploits a simple asymmetry: professional analyses are difficult to solve because the relevant evidence must first be found and interpreted, but much easier to verify once that evidence is fixed. During task synthesis, the engine constructs a reference analysis from source evidence and asks an independent agent to reproduce its conclusions from the same evidence without seeing it. Only after the analysis is verified is it compiled into an open-ended task with an item-level scoring contract, allowing the same task to support both evaluation and training. We apply VADE across four professional domains; in an independent expert review of 186 finance tasks, 93.5% meet a high bar for source fidelity, answer correctness, and evaluation fairness. In finance, these tasks expose substantial remaining model errors, particularly unsupported facts and inferences, while training on verified solver trajectories improves held-out performance and yields gains that transfer to public finance benchmarks such as Finance Agent Benchmark v2. Together, these results suggest a practical path toward scalable, verifiable supervision for open-ended professional tasks.
researchers.summary: VADE builds verifiable analysis tasks for agents in law/finance from public professional sources, exploiting that answers are hard to find but easy to verify.

researchers.title: A Matrix Lee-Sidford Barrier and Faster Semidefinite Programming
researchers.abstract: We construct a matrix analog of the Lee-Sidford barrier for semidefinite programming (SDP) with $m$ equality constraints and $n$-by-$n$ matrices. The barrier has self-concordance parameter $\widetilde{O}(m)$, so short-step interior-point methods require only $\widetilde O(\sqrt m)$ iterations. We also show that our matrix Lee-Sidford barrier can be implemented efficiently by developing a randomized algorithm that solves SDPs with $m\leq n$ to accuracy $\epsilon$ in $(n^{\omega+o(1)}+n^2m^{3/2+o(1)})\operatorname{polylog}(1/\epsilon)$ time, where $\omega\leq 9/4$ is the matrix multiplication exponent, achieving the fastest known running time in this regime.
researchers.evidence: 'Independent Researcher' affiliation, frequent co-author Ruizhe Zhang
researchers.summary: A matrix analogue of the Lee-Sidford barrier with self-concordance Õ(m), giving the fastest known SDP solver for m ≤ n.

papers.title: Training Dynamics of Large State-Transition Models
papers.abstract: Next-token prediction relies on learned token embeddings whose dimension $d$ is much smaller than the vocabulary size $V$. Existing analyses of training dynamics either fix the embeddings with $d\ge V$ or train them only in restricted settings. It remains unclear whether jointly training the embeddings by gradient-based methods from random initialization leads to accurate prediction when $d<V$. In this paper, we study this question in the simplest setting where it is already nontrivial, namely next-token prediction with a one-token context, which we refer to as a state-transition model. The model consists of an input embedding and an output embedding, either untied or tied, and is trained from Gaussian initialization by perturbed gradient descent with weight decay on the population cross-entropy loss. We consider ground-truth transition laws whose centered log-probability table has low rank and bounded entries, and measure the prediction quality by the relative prediction gain (RPG). It is zero for the uniform predictor and one for the optimal predictor. For the untied model, we show that when $d=\Omega(\sqrt V)$, with probability at least $1-e^{-cd}$ for some constant $c$, the RPG is above $7/8$ at every iterate in the final $1-1/d$ fraction of training iterations. For the tied model trained on a subset of states, we prove that the RPG on the observed states is $1-O(V/d^2)$, and under a coverage condition on the ground truth and a bound on the learned embeddings, we further prove a prediction guarantee on the unseen states. Our analysis is based on the bounded trace of the Hessian of the softmax cross-entropy loss, which implies that the approximate second-order stationary points reached by training have high prediction gain. Numerical experiments with practical parameter choices illustrate the persistent training gain and the transfer of the tied model.
papers.summary: Next-token prediction with a one-token context (a 'state-transition model') where input and output embeddings of dimension d < V are trained jointly from Gaussian init by perturbed GD with weight decay on population cross-entropy. For a low-rank centred log-probability table, the untied model reaches relative prediction gain > 7/8 once d = Ω(√V); the tied model gets 1 − O(V/d²) on observed states plus a transfer guarantee to unseen states. The key tool is a bound on the trace of the softmax-CE Hessian at approximate second-order stationary points.
papers.why: A rigorous learning-dynamics result for factorized softmax over a large vocabulary with d < V, which is the regime his GR memorization paper needs to cite and compare with.

papers.title: Grammar Sparsity Sets How Transformers Learn Random Languages
papers.comments: 13 pages, 11 figures. Accepted at NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Principles of Generative Modeling
papers.abstract: We study language acquisition by transformers trained on the Random Language Model: a synthetic hierarchical grammar with random production rules, whose sparsity is controlled by a single parameter and whose conditional entropies are known exactly. On depth-two grammars, we find that sparsity sets both the order and the speed of learning. Dense grammars are learnt one level at a time: a token is predicted from its sibling after $t\propto V$ steps and from the full context only after $t\propto V^{3}$, so the two stages are separated by a plateau that widens with $V$. Sparse grammars are learnt all at once, at $t\propto\sqrt V$, with a smaller exponent than even the first stage of a dense one. The exponents $1$ and $1/2$ already appear at depth one, where we derive them for a linear model trained with Adam.
papers.summary: Transformers trained on the Random Language Model (random hierarchical grammar with known conditional entropies). Dense grammars are learnt level by level: sibling-based prediction after t ∝ V steps, full-context only after t ∝ V^3, with a widening plateau in between; sparse grammars are learnt all at once at t ∝ √V. The exponents 1 and 1/2 are derived at depth one for a linear model trained with Adam.
papers.why: Sharp scaling of learning time with vocabulary on hierarchical data, with a solvable linear-model piece; a template for level-by-level learning of a docid tree.

papers.title: Statistical mechanics of linear classification on hierarchical tree data
papers.abstract: Deep networks owe much of their success to their ability to exploit the structure in data, from the grammar of language to the multi-scale organization of images. Yet, many statistical mechanics approaches to structured data rely on Gaussian equivalence, whose assumptions can fail when a few latent variables influence all input coordinates. In this work, we take a step beyond this setting with a simple setup, in which a linear classifier is trained to infer the root of the classical broadcast process on a tree from its $N$ leaves. Despite this simplicity, the data already display non-Gaussian statistics along the direction carrying the label, as well as strong finite-size effects. By retaining the exact law along this direction and approximating the transverse fluctuations as Gaussian, we obtain a finite-depth replica theory that accurately describes the measured learning curves. At large depth and sufficiently weak regularization, we uncover a double descent whose two stages are separated in scale. In a range of broadcast noise below the reconstruction threshold, the first descent occurs at a number of samples scaling as $N^\omega$, with $0<\omega<1$ set by the data statistics, whereas the overfitting peak occurs at order $N$ samples. Beyond linear classifiers, this setup could serve as a controlled starting point to study deeper architectures and generative models on hierarchical data.
papers.summary: A linear classifier is trained to infer the root of a broadcast process on a tree from its N leaves. Keeping the exact non-Gaussian law along the label direction and treating transverse fluctuations as Gaussian gives a finite-depth replica theory that matches learning curves. At large depth there is a double descent whose first descent occurs at N^ω samples (0<ω<1) and whose overfitting peak occurs at order N.
papers.why: Solvable model of learning on tree-structured data beyond Gaussian equivalence; background for the tree paper.

papers.title: Vanishing Initialization Turns Diagonal Tensor Gradient Flow into Greedy Matching
papers.abstract: We study gradient-flow (GF) learning of tensors from vanishing initialization in canonical polyadic (CP) factorization models. For tensors of order $\nu\geq3$ whose targets are diagonal in mode-wise orthonormal bases, we prove that the limiting learning dynamics follows a simple greedy bipartite matching process. Each rank-one component of the model, called an atom, can potentially learn each rank-one component of the target, called a scalar sector. Every atom--sector pair has an initialization-dependent activation clock, representing the time at which the atom would grow to macroscopic size in that sector if the pair evolved in isolation. Processing these clocks in increasing order and selecting a pair whenever neither its atom nor its sector has been selected before determines the sequence of actual learning events. We prove that the GF trajectory converges to the corresponding staircase of learned target components. The task of learning modular addition by a CP model with complex weights falls exactly into this framework after Fourier diagonalization. Its activation clocks are independent and identically distributed, allowing us to combine the GF reduction with known random matching asymptotics and derive an explicit, distribution-free large-system loss curve after time reparametrization. We also obtain an asymptotic formula relating this curve to the original GF training time. For models with real weights, conjugate Fourier modes instead form two-dimensional blocks with richer internal structure. We characterize their rank and border-rank cascade and conjecture that the corresponding GF dynamics follows interleaved multi-stage learning processes.
papers.summary: Gradient flow on CP tensor factorization (order ≥ 3, diagonal target in orthonormal bases) from vanishing initialization is proved to follow a greedy bipartite matching between model atoms and target components, ordered by initialization-dependent activation clocks, giving a staircase loss. Modular addition fits after Fourier diagonalization, yielding an explicit distribution-free large-system loss curve.
papers.why: Clean incremental-learning (saddle-to-saddle) theorem; same flavour as sequential learning of classes in his GR dynamics.

papers.title: Global Stability and Loss Convergence in Matrix Factorization
papers.abstract: We study the matrix factorization objective $\mathcal L(X,Y)=f(XY)$ for convex, twice continuously differentiable output losses with bounded and Lipschitz gradient and a minimizing set that is compact modulo specified input and output invariances. This includes the well-known cross entropy loss. We prove that a positive learning-rate threshold guarantees bounded parameters, summability of squared gradients, and convergence of the loss from every finite initialization. The proof constructs a quantity from the imbalance between parameter matrices that decreases over every step of the gradient descent trajectory.
papers.summary: For L(X,Y) = f(XY) with convex, smooth, Lipschitz-gradient f (including cross-entropy) and a minimizing set compact modulo invariances, GD with a learning rate below a positive threshold keeps parameters bounded, has summable squared gradients and converges in loss from every finite initialization. The proof uses a decreasing imbalance quantity between the two factors.
papers.why: Global convergence for factorized cross-entropy (embedding times unembedding), the model class behind softmax-based retrieval.

papers.title: Grokking as a Subspace Search: Computing the Destination Before Training
papers.abstract: Grokking is the phenomenon in which a neural network generalizes long after it has memorized its training data. Many explanations have been proposed for the delay between memorization and generalization. However, none of them can say before training where the network is heading, so they cannot be tested against one another. We show that on group tasks this destination can be computed from the task itself before training begins. It is a low-dimensional subspace of the network's embeddings, which we call the right subspace, and we prove that it is essentially unique. Knowing the destination makes our hypothesis falsifiable: the delay is a search for the right subspace, and generalization begins when the network finds it. When we give the network the right subspace from the start, the delay disappears. When we take the right subspace away, accuracy stops at a ceiling that we compute before training, and on multiplication the network cannot generalize at all. When we train the network normally, its embeddings move toward the right subspace by themselves, long before test accuracy rises. Finally, interventions during training show that this search sets the length of the delay, and that noise in the optimization does not. On every group task that we tested, grokking is a search for the right subspace, and the delay is the time that this search takes.
papers.summary: On group tasks, the low-dimensional embedding subspace a grokking network ends in can be computed from the task before training and is shown to be essentially unique. Giving the network this subspace removes the delay; removing it caps accuracy at a precomputable ceiling; during normal training embeddings drift toward it long before test accuracy rises.
papers.why: A falsifiable account of the grokking delay with interventions.

papers.title: Pretraining Representation Lottery Determines Fine-tuning Generalization
papers.abstract: Large scale pretraining (PT) followed by fine-tuning (FT) is the central paradigm of modern deep learning, yet how PT shapes FT generalization remains poorly understood. We use a synthetic setup in which the ground-truth concept geometry of entities is known, as a controlled testbed to study how representational geometry affects model behavior and how PT representations determine FT generalization. We first show that models differing only in training seed can closely match in PT loss yet vary substantially in FT generalization. We hypothesize that a representational lottery underlies this phenomenon: the random seed dependent geometry formed during PT determines what FT can reach. We confirm this causally. First, injecting the ground-truth concept geometry into the model yields near-ceiling FT generalization, showing that good representations directly drive generalization. Then, distilling a lucky seed's learned representation into an unlucky seed unlocks FT generalization, while distilling the same model's behavior does not. Furthermore, representation distillation can merge entities that never interacted during PT, which FT alone cannot. Finally, we show that regularizing representational drift during FT enables naturalistic learning: only models with good representations learn the task, and they generalize, while models with poor representations fail to fit it. Under plain FT, by contrast, models with poor representations fit the training objective by reshaping their pretrained representations. We reproduce the distillation result in Pythia-160M and Pythia-410M, each pretrained multiple times with different random seeds, and show that the transferable representation lives in the deep layers at both scales. Overall, PT acts as a lottery over representations, and the representation a model draws determines how it adapts during FT in a way that behavior alone does not explain.
papers.summary: In a synthetic setup with known concept geometry, seeds with equal pretraining loss differ widely in fine-tuning generalization. Injecting the true geometry, or distilling a lucky seed's representation (not its behaviour) into an unlucky one, fixes fine-tuning; reproduced on multi-seed Pythia-160M/410M, where the transferable representation lives in deep layers.
papers.why: Controlled evidence that pretraining geometry, not loss, decides what fine-tuning can reach.

papers.title: Hidden Sensitivity in LLM Pre-training: A Dynamic System View
papers.abstract: In Large Language Model (LLM) pre-training, loss curves can conceal substantial instability, i.e., even small perturbations may lead to dramatically different predictions while leaving loss nearly unchanged. To investigate this phenomenon and reveal the underlying mechanisms, we first formulate LLM pre-training as a non-autonomous dynamical system that jointly evolves model weights and Adam optimizer states. Based on this formulation, we introduce a normalized sensitivity score in optimizer-relative coordinates to identify sensitive training checkpoints. At one such checkpoint, a weight perturbation of only 10^(-5) leads to 35.7% disagreement in top-1 predictions and 16.2% disagreement in benchmark answers after 200 training steps, with only 0.8% of greedy generations remaining identical despite similar validation losses. Furthermore, we find that perturbations to Adam's first and second moments induce comparably large effects, with similar sensitivity patterns observed in OLMo-1B. Finally, guided by our diagnostic, targeted stabilization reduces top-1 disagreement to 0.83% and increases generation exact match to 88.3%, at the cost of a 0.11-nat increase in validation loss. Our findings reveal a hidden form of optimizer-state-dependent sensitivity in LLM pre-training that conventional loss-based evaluations may overlook, while demonstrating its potential for diagnosis and mitigation.
papers.summary: Treats LLM pretraining as a non-autonomous dynamical system over weights and Adam states. At sensitive checkpoints a 1e-5 weight perturbation yields 35.7% top-1 disagreement after 200 steps with nearly equal validation loss; perturbing Adam moments has similar effects (also in OLMo-1B). A targeted stabilization cuts disagreement to 0.83% at a 0.11-nat loss cost.
papers.why: A clean, measurable instability that loss curves hide.

papers.title: What Makes Recurrence Generalize Across Lengths?
papers.comments: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on AXIOM: Foundations of Efficient Deep Learning
papers.abstract: Multi-step reasoning requires models to preserve and update intermediate information as computation unfolds. State tracking captures this fundamental requirement, but models that succeed within a fixed range of state transitions may not generalize when substantially more updates are required. Recurrent Transformers offer a natural mechanism for addressing this challenge by repeatedly applying shared Transformer blocks, allowing computation to scale with problem length. We study when such recurrent computation generalizes beyond the training range in a controlled state-tracking task, varying operation representation, positional encoding, and recurrent capacity. We find that recurrence alone is insufficient: multi-token template representations and absolute positional encoding can severely limit extrapolation, whereas atomic operation representations enable substantially stronger length generalization. The effect of positional structure also varies with recurrent depth, with periodic positional encoding achieving the strongest mean performance at greater recurrent depth. Most importantly, scaling the recurrent operator extends the extrapolation horizon, reaching 35.1% exact-match accuracy on sequences of 20-40 operations after training only on 2-10, while substantially larger fixed-depth Transformers remain at 0%. Additional recurrent computation at test time can extend the range over which the model generalizes, but does not eliminate failure on much longer sequences. These results suggest that recurrent computation can support length-generalizable state tracking, but that its effectiveness depends critically on whether the learned computation remains reusable across sequence lengths.
papers.summary: Controlled state-tracking study of recurrent (weight-shared) transformers: atomic operation tokens extrapolate far better than multi-token templates, absolute positions hurt, and scaling the recurrent operator gives 35.1% exact match on 20-40 operations after training on 2-10, where larger fixed-depth transformers get 0%.
papers.why: Which design choices make looped computation length-generalize, measured cleanly.

papers.title: Can Latent Reasoning Drive LLM Outputs Without a Trace?
papers.abstract: LLMs typically solve complex tasks with chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning, which is also the main tool for monitoring them for misaligned behavior. However, standard transformers can also solve tasks with complete latent reasoning (CLR), carrying out the whole task internally and outputting only the final answer. Theory bounds the depth of CLR, the number of sequential steps it can carry out, and recent work measured it to be shallow. In this work, we ask whether CLR is deep enough for a model to pursue a hidden objective that requires reasoning. Such a model would generate a CoT that appears to solve the given task, while a latent multi-step computation decides its answer based on the hidden objective. First, we show that a simple auxiliary loss allows models to solve a multi-step task latently at least 5x deeper than previously reported. Then, in two common tasks, decision-making and code generation, we train a model to pursue such a hidden objective, which decides a loan or plants a vulnerability. The model's CoT justifies the output with no trace of the hidden objective, and a strong LLM monitor does not flag it. Finally, using activation patching, we find that the latent computation is completed before the model generates its CoT, which takes no part in it. Altogether, we show that a hidden objective that requires reasoning can go unseen by a monitor that reads only the output.
papers.summary: With an auxiliary loss, transformers solve multi-step tasks fully latently at least 5x deeper than previously reported. Models trained to pursue a hidden objective (loan decisions, planting a code vulnerability) write CoTs with no trace of it, and activation patching shows the latent computation finishes before the CoT is generated.
papers.why: Empirical upper end of no-CoT latent depth, relevant to expressivity bounds on latent reasoning.

papers.title: Character Information in Language Models: A Prompt-Independent Word Store and a Late, Question-Driven Signal That Grows With Scale
papers.abstract: Linear probes recover character properties of a word from a language model's hidden states, but a probe at the answer position cannot say whether the property was stored with the word or produced because the prompt asked for it. We separate the two with a word-position baseline: the same held-out-word probe applied to the query word's own tokens in a sentence that asks nothing. Across 16 open-weight models from seven families (0.6B--14B) and eleven character tasks, the word tokens encode \texttt{first\_letter}, \texttt{last\_letter} and \texttt{most\_frequent\_letter} above a word-only nuisance floor in all 16 models, and about 70\% of that signal is already present in the token embedding. Asking the question adds a second signal at the answer position. Its size grows with model scale for all four prompt-sensitive tasks (Holm-corrected permutation $p \leq 0.018$, also within model families), and the growth is confined to the late layers: restricted to the first quarter of the network, the slope is indistinguishable from zero. Small models' answer positions hold less linearly decodable signal than their word-level store; large models' hold more. Four controls bound these claims. Measured against the nuisance floor, the question-free signal that a majority-baseline analysis counts as retained largely disappears (\texttt{last\_letter}: $-0.01$). Count tasks become measurable only after length, repetition and query-letter shortcuts are removed by design. A pre-registered test finds that a question placed before the word does not change the word's own encoding beyond what an arbitrary prefix change does. Representation--readout gaps show no robust scaling once probe saturation is accounted for. Pre-registered criteria, a fixed estimator (held-out layer selection, cold-start folds) and all analysis code accompany the paper.
papers.summary: Across 16 models (0.6B-14B), first/last/most-frequent letter of a word is linearly decodable from the word's own tokens with no question asked, ~70% already in the token embedding. Asking the question adds a second, late-layer signal at the answer position whose size grows with scale; controls remove length/repetition shortcuts.
papers.why: Careful separation of stored vs question-driven character knowledge, relevant to tokenization questions.

papers.title: From Learning Rates to Rotational Schedules: Finite-Horizon Theory on the Sphere
papers.abstract: How should step sizes be scheduled across a finite training horizon? Cosine and warmup-stable-decay (WSD) schedules are widely adopted in large-scale pretraining, yet their effect on optimization also depends on parameter norms. Normalization can make parameter groups scale invariant, so that the loss depends only on their direction, while their norms still affect how fast the parameters rotate. In this work, we formulate schedule design directly in the space of rotational motion. Working within a geodesically convex spherical setting, we derive a last-iterate convergence guarantee for arbitrary rotational schedules that separates their overall scale from their distribution over time. We derive the unique schedule that minimizes this bound and prove that it approaches linear decay as the horizon grows. Empirically, our rotational interpretation and idealized spherical analysis provide useful predictions for LLM pretraining in practice, including schedule comparisons missed by existing analyses. Our analysis predicts schedule ordering across model scales for both vanilla (Adam, Muon) and Hyperball-style (AdamH, MuonH) optimizers. Our Hyperball experiments support the predicted strong performance of linear LR decay and confirm our prediction that WSD underperforms in this setting. Accounting for parameter norm dynamics, we predict instead the strong performance of WSD for Adam and Muon shown in practice. Guided by our theoretical insights, we also derive a new LR schedule for Adam and Muon, which improves over the established cosine and WSD schedules. All in all, these results support the use of rotational dynamics to understand, predict, and ultimately guide scheduling in LLM pretraining.
papers.summary: Rewrites learning-rate schedules as rotational schedules for scale-invariant (normalized) parameters. In a geodesically convex spherical setting, a last-iterate bound separates the schedule's scale from its time profile; the optimal schedule tends to linear decay. Predictions about WSD vs linear decay for Adam/Muon vs their hyperball variants hold in LLM pretraining, and give a new schedule that beats cosine and WSD.
papers.why: Theory that predicts LLM schedule rankings.

papers.title: How Multi-Timescale Memory Cools Optimization: Theory and Evidence from AdEMAMix
papers.abstract: Augmenting AdamW with multiple momentum timescales improves large language model pretraining, yet the mechanism driving these gains remains poorly understood. We identify an interaction between multi-timescale optimizer memory and the geometry of normalized networks: memory changes parameter norms and thereby controls how fast parameters rotate. Starting from exact norm dynamics under decoupled weight decay, we show that the parameter norm depends on the temporal correlation of the updates, with weight decay controlling how long these correlations influence optimization. We show how an independently weighted slow momentum can substantially increase the norm of parameters, while contributing negligible power to the instantaneous update, therefore acting as an endogenous annealing schedule. We study this mechanism in AdEMAMix for language-model pretraining. Controlled interventions show that this scheduling mechanism has clear practical consequences and is an important factor behind AdEMAMix's advantage over AdamW.
papers.summary: Explains AdEMAMix's gain over AdamW through norm dynamics under decoupled weight decay: a slow momentum barely changes the instantaneous update but inflates parameter norms, slowing rotation and acting as an endogenous annealing schedule; controlled interventions in LM pretraining support this.
papers.why: Mechanistic optimizer explanation via parameter norms; companion to the rotational-schedule paper.

papers.title: SGD Selects Initialization-Dependent Representation in Overparameterized ReLU Networks
papers.abstract: Overparameterized neural networks can represent the same function through many different hidden configurations, raising the question of which representation is favored by a given training algorithm. We study how stochastic gradient descent (SGD), jointly training both layers, resolves this ambiguity in finite-width, bias-free, two-layer ReLU networks trained to learn a linear teacher under Gaussian inputs. At width two, exact fitting leaves no choice: the neurons must align with the teacher directions. At every width $m \ge 4$, however, infinitely many non-aligned exact fits are possible. Despite this ambiguity, we prove that joint batch-size-one SGD from sufficiently small initialization drives every neuron arbitrarily close to one of the two teacher directions while reaching arbitrarily small population error in finite time. This occurs without explicit regularization, layerwise training, gradient clipping, or a learning-rate schedule. The dynamics additionally select an initialization-dependent allocation of the fitted function across neurons, providing a finer characterization of the representation selected by SGD. Numerical experiments reproduce the predicted alignment, fitting, and initialization-dependent allocation. Our results identify sufficient conditions under which standard SGD exhibits a strong implicit bias toward a highly structured internal representation, even when overparameterization creates infinitely many qualitatively different exact representations.
papers.summary: Two-layer bias-free ReLU nets of width m ≥ 4 learning a linear teacher under Gaussian inputs have infinitely many non-aligned exact fits, yet batch-size-one SGD from small init provably drives every neuron to one of the two teacher directions and reaches arbitrarily small error in finite time, with an init-dependent allocation across neurons.
papers.why: Implicit bias of plain SGD toward a structured representation, proved at finite width.

papers.title: Learning the Projection onto the Data Support: Distribution Learning that Avoids Memorization
papers.abstract: We introduce a framework for learning distributions supported on manifolds based on estimating the nearest-point projection onto the data support. Specifically, we define an objective functional over a class of functions whose minimizer recovers this projection. The proposed framework automatically adapts to the intrinsic dimension and allows for data supported on unions of manifolds with varying dimensions. The resulting objective can be optimized using standard neural network architectures. We present population-level results establishing recovery of the manifold projection and prove finite-sample Wasserstein generalization bounds. Furthermore, we validate the approach empirically across a range of settings. In contrast to widely used generative models such as diffusion models, whose objectives can be minimized by memorizing training samples, our formulation excludes such behavior. We also introduce a direct memorization metric to verify that the learned projection generates new samples rather than reproducing the training set.
papers.summary: Learns distributions on (unions of) manifolds by estimating the nearest-point projection onto the data support via an objective whose minimizer is that projection; it adapts to intrinsic dimension, has finite-sample Wasserstein bounds, and, unlike diffusion objectives, cannot be minimized by memorizing training samples.
papers.why: A generative objective that provably excludes memorization.

papers.title: Data-Dependent Probability Estimation via Sample Amplification
papers.abstract: Can we estimate the probability of an event chosen after seeing the data, without using any fresh samples? Its empirical probability can be arbitrarily misleading, while learning the entire distribution to constant accuracy requires $\Theta(d)$ samples on a domain of size $d$. We show that $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{d})$ samples suffice for constant mean squared error, provided the rule choosing the event is known. More generally, our estimator handles arbitrary $[0,1]$-valued queries and runs in polynomial time given evaluation access to the rule. This sample complexity matches the known lower bound up to logarithmic factors and resolves the open question posed by Feldman, Kale, Raman, Talwar, and Tewari (arXiv:2610.41244). Our estimation framework relies on a new combination of sample amplification (arXiv:1904.12053 and arXiv:2201.04315) with distribution learning via online optimization. Our estimator achieves mean squared error $O(d^{3/4}/n)$ when $d\leq n$ and $\widetilde{O}(d^{1/4}/\sqrt{n})$ when $d>n$. We complement this with a lower bound of $\Omega(\min\{1,\sqrt{d}/n\})$ on the mean squared error. Using our framework, we also design an efficient estimator for data-dependent queries on Gaussian distributions with unknown mean and identity covariance. Finally, we show that a smoothed variant of the problem is much (exponentially) easier. For discrete distributions, if the sample size is chosen uniformly from $\{n,\ldots,2n-1\}$, then $n=O(\log d)$ suffices for constant mean squared error.
papers.summary: Estimating the probability of an event chosen after seeing the data, with no fresh samples: Õ(√d) samples suffice for constant MSE on a domain of size d when the selection rule is known, matching the lower bound up to logs and resolving an open question of Feldman et al. Uses sample amplification plus online-learning distribution estimation; a smoothed variant needs only O(log d).
papers.why: Sharp answer to a clean adaptive-data-analysis question.

papers.title: Deterministic Proper Positive-Only Learning Is Independent of ZFC
papers.abstract: Binary classification from positive-only samples is a variant of PAC learning in which the learner receives i.i.d. samples only from the positive region of an unknown target concept, but is evaluated on the full distribution. Improper learnability in this model has a textbook characterization, whereas proper learnability has remained open for decades. Recent work characterized it for learners with access to randomness, and showed that, unlike in PAC learning, some classes are properly learnable with randomness but not without it, leaving the deterministic case open. We show that this case cannot be resolved within the standard axioms of mathematics (ZFC): there is a class of VC dimension two whose deterministic proper learnability is independent of ZFC, even though a randomized learner provably learns it. Moreover, no dimension of finite character, a desirable property shared by most dimensions in learning theory, characterizes deterministic proper learnability. We also show that the size of the domain is decisive. In ZFC, deterministic proper learnability has a combinatorial characterization on every domain whose cardinality is below a certain threshold, including every countable domain. In contrast, this characterization fails on every domain of sufficiently large cardinality. Under the generalized continuum hypothesis, this threshold is sharp: it is the exact cardinality at which the characterization starts to fail. Finally, our proofs introduce new tools, based on the Erdos--Rado partition theorem, that may be of broader interest.
papers.summary: Deterministic proper PAC learnability from positive-only samples is independent of ZFC: a VC-dimension-2 class exists whose deterministic proper learnability is undecidable although a randomized learner learns it, and no finite-character dimension characterizes it. Below a cardinality threshold (including countable domains) a combinatorial characterization holds; under GCH the threshold is sharp.
papers.why: A clean, surprising learning-theory result (Ben-David et al.).

papers.title: The Value of Labels in Data Selection for Least Squares
papers.abstract: Suppose a selector sees a finite labelled dataset and chooses $n$ of its rows, with repetition. Ordinary least squares is then fitted to the rows that were chosen, without weights, and the excess loss of the fit on the full dataset is measured in units of the optimal loss. Without further assumptions this ratio does not decay with $n$. We examine the problem for $d$ features and rows of normalized leverage at most $\kappa$, and determine or bound the leading constants. A selector that must establish its rule before seeing the labels has an optimal worst-case ratio of $d\kappa/n$ to leading order, whatever use it makes of the features. With scalar labels, a selector that sees the labels achieves a value between $d\kappa/(2n)$ and $d\kappa\Lambda_d/n$, where $\Lambda_d<1$ is the rounding constant of mean selection. For $d\le4$, the constant is then $d\kappa/2$, so that labels are worth exactly a factor of two there, and for one feature and $m$ outputs it is $\kappa\Lambda_m$. With two or more features the selector can change the proportions of the frequent rows and therefore reshape its own design matrix. We design a simplified optimization problem, which we call a game, that bounds the constant for datasets with exactly fitted frequent rows, then show that its value is at most one half of the gradient energy in several regimes, and that one half is exact along directions in which the frequent rows are rigid, such as an intercept. For grouped designs, in which reshaping amounts to the allocation of a common budget, the constant is $27d/128$ up to an additive constant, compared with $d$ without labels. Nevertheless, one half is not the constant in every dimension: we construct datasets of extremely high dimension and large leverage on which every selection has an excess ratio of at least $(e^{-1/2}-o(1))\,d\kappa/n$, so that labels are worth at most a factor close to $\sqrt e$ there.
papers.summary: Choosing n rows of a dataset (rows of leverage ≤ κ) to fit unweighted OLS: a label-blind selector has optimal worst-case excess ratio dκ/n, while one that sees labels gets between dκ/(2n) and dκΛ_d/n, so labels are worth exactly a factor 2 for d ≤ 4; for grouped designs the constant is 27d/128, and a high-dimensional construction shows labels are worth at most ~√e there.
papers.why: Exact constants for the value of labels in data selection.

papers.title: Tight Mistake-Abstention Tradeoffs for Sequential Prediction under Adversarial Injections
papers.abstract: We study the sequential prediction problem introduced by Goel et al. (2023), where an adversary can inject arbitrarily many corrupted instances in an i.i.d. stream from a clean distribution $\mu$, while the learner is allowed to abstain from making a prediction at no cost if the current instance was indeed injected. When $\mu$ is unknown, Yu and Blanchard (2026) show a polynomial tradeoff between mistakes and false abstentions for classes with finite VC dimension and oblivious adversaries, but still leave open a significant gap between upper and lower bounds in their tradeoff landscape. In this paper, we propose the weighted shattering potential, and based on variants of this potential, provide gap-closing algorithms that essentially characterize the tradeoffs under various settings of interest: When $\mu$ is known, our algorithm improves over Goel et al. (2023) and achieves their conjectured $O(d\log T)$ mistake bound; When $\mu$ is unknown, for oblivious adversary, our guarantees are tight both in $T$ and in terms of the VC dimension $d$, which completely characterizes the abstention-mistake tradeoff in this setting and gives an $O(\sqrt{dT})$ balanced rate. For adaptive adversary, our results are tight up to $\operatorname{poly}(dD\log T)$ factors for structured classes with finite so-called reduction dimension $D$. Our guarantees also extend to censored feedback, where the label is hidden after an abstention.
papers.summary: Sequential prediction with adversarially injected instances and free abstention on injected points: a weighted-shattering potential gives the conjectured O(d log T) mistakes for known μ, and tight-in-T-and-d mistake/abstention tradeoffs (balanced rate O(√(dT))) for unknown μ and oblivious adversaries.
papers.why: Closes the gap in a clean online-learning tradeoff.

papers.title: Tight Bounds for Rank Estimation in Turnstile Streams
papers.comments: 54 pages, 3 figures. The abstract is abridged to meet arXiv's length limit
papers.abstract: We study rank estimation in turnstile streams. A frequency vector $f$ over the universe $[U]$ receives insertions and deletions. Given a query $x\in[U]$, the goal is to estimate the rank $\sum_{u<x}f_u$ within additive error $\epsilon\|f\|_1$ with constant probability. The standard approach is Dyadic CountSketch by Luo, Wang, Yi and Cormode, using $\tilde{O}(\epsilon^{-1}\log^{3/2}U\log n)$ bits, where $n$ is the final $\ell_1$ norm of $f$. Bul\'anek, Kumar, Meka, Nelson, and Sarl\'os placed this approach in a matrix-factorization framework. They improved the space of Dyadic CountSketch to $O(\epsilon^{-1}\log^{3/2}U)$ words, and proved a lower bound of $\Omega(\epsilon^{-1}\log^2(\epsilon U))$ bits for all streaming algorithms when $U\le n\le U^{O(1)}$ and $\epsilon=U^{-1+\Omega(1)}$. This leaves a gap of $\sqrt{\log U}$. In this work, we fully determine the space cost of rank estimation up to an absolute constant. Our main result is a space lower bound for all streaming algorithms: for $0<\epsilon\le 1/8$ and $n\ge\log^2 U$, the space is at least $\Omega(\min\{\epsilon^{-1}L^{3/2}\log(2+n\epsilon/\sqrt{L}), \epsilon^{-2}\log U\log n, \log\binom{U+n}{n}\})$ bits, where $L=\log(2+U\epsilon)$. When $U\le n\le U^{O(1)}$ and $\epsilon=U^{-1+\Omega(1)}$, this simplifies to $\Omega(\min\{\epsilon^{-1}\log^{5/2}U, \epsilon^{-2}\log^2 U\})$ bits. Our proof uses a surprising hard distribution and novel information-theoretic techniques. The above bound matches Dyadic CountSketch when $n\ge U$ and $U^{-1+\Omega(1)}\le\epsilon\le O(1/\sqrt{\log U})$. The lower bound is also tight in the remaining regimes. For $\epsilon\ge(\log U)^{-1/2}$, there exists an algorithm that uses $O(\epsilon^{-2}\log U\log n)$ bits using $\ell_1$ samplers. For $\epsilon\le U^{-1+o(1)}$, we refine Dyadic CountSketch so that its space in bits matches the first term of the bound.
papers.summary: Determines the space complexity of rank (quantile) estimation in turnstile streams up to a constant: a new lower bound Ω(min{ε^{-1}L^{3/2}log(…), ε^{-2}log U log n, …}) bits that matches Dyadic CountSketch in its regime, with refined algorithms for the remaining regimes.
papers.why: Tight sketching bound; sketching lower-bound techniques port to retrieval.

papers.title: The abc index: Exact Retrieval for Learned Sparse Representations
papers.abstract: In learned sparse retrieval (LSR), queries have tens of terms with learned weights, on which classic dynamic pruning is believed to fail, and approximate indexes such as Seismic and HNSW are considered faster than exact ones. We challenge this view with abc, an exact index built only from standard IR techniques: term-at-a-time (TAAT) evaluation, Block-Max MaxScore, binary packing and doc-id reordering. They are combined in a new design and engineered for modern CPUs. On MS MARCO encoded with four LSR models, the abc index is the fastest exact index at every k: 6.5-84x faster than the exact search of Qdrant, 13-55x faster than that of Lucene, and 2.9-18x faster than BMP with an index 5-7x smaller. Against approximate indexes, it takes 1.5-3.6x less space, and its latency grows much more slowly with k: they are up to 4.3x faster at k=10, but at k=1000 it overtakes them, by up to 7.4x. Exactness comes with an extra benefit: there are no parameters to tune.
papers.summary: abc, an exact index for learned sparse retrieval built from standard parts (TAAT, Block-Max MaxScore, binary packing, doc-id reordering). On MS MARCO with four LSR models it is the fastest exact index (6.5-84x Qdrant, 2.9-18x BMP) and, while approximate indexes (Seismic, HNSW) are up to 4.3x faster at k=10, it overtakes them by up to 7.4x at k=1000 with 1.5-3.6x less space.

papers.title: Look Before You Leap: Re-Architecting Disk-Resident Vector Search with TriVS
papers.abstract: Disk-resident approximate nearest-neighbor search (ANNS) scales vector search beyond DRAM, yet state-of-the-art systems remain I/O-bound, even with fast SSDs and sophisticated I/O execution. To understand this bottleneck, we conduct an I/O-centric analysis that breaks each query down into an approach phase that locates a query-near region and a converge phase that resolves the final top-k. This analysis reveals complementary I/O tradeoffs: cluster-based search circumvents approach-phase I/O through in-memory routing but reads coarse-grained, full clusters during convergence, whereas graph-based search employs fine-grained, vector-level I/O throughout, enabling efficient convergence at the cost of inevitable I/O during the approach phase. To combine the complementary I/O benefits of the two granularities, we present TriVS, a new paradigm that re-architects disk-resident vector search as a trilogy: approach coarsely, distill progressively, and converge exactly. Its key innovations come in two parts. First, it decouples the approach and converge phases from a single search granularity, employing cluster-based search to avoid approach-phase I/O and leveraging vector-level I/O for efficient convergence. Second, to bridge the two granularities, it introduces a new in-memory distill phase between the original two, progressively reducing routed clusters to a vector-level shortlist using compact quantized vectors before disk access. Moreover, coarser clustering shrinks the centroid-routing index, allowing TriVS to reallocate existing memory to distillation rather than expand its memory budget. Our evaluation on five datasets spanning diverse vector types and scales shows that, at Recall@10=0.9, TriVS achieves on average 3.42X PipeANN's throughput, 51.2% lower latency, and 63.7% less disk I/O, while using less memory and storage than PipeANN.
papers.summary: TriVS for disk-resident ANN: route coarsely with in-memory clusters (no approach-phase I/O), distill routed clusters to a shortlist with compact quantized vectors in memory, then converge with vector-level disk reads. 3.42x PipeANN throughput at Recall@10 = 0.9 with less memory and 64% less I/O.

papers.title: Zarc: Exact Nearest Neighbors over a Billion Vectors in Seconds
papers.abstract: Exact k-nearest-neighbor vector search lies on the critical path of machine learning systems, from sparse attention in the latest large language models (LLMs) to long-context memories and training-data deduplication. Exhaustive GPU search scans the whole dataset for every query, while approximate indexes return inexact neighbors. Recent methods skip almost every vector with a cheap half-precision proof that it lies too far away, but only on one GPU that holds the whole dataset. Our insight is to keep only the short rows of these proofs in GPU memory and to fetch the few remaining full vectors from host memory. Our system, Zarc, answers Euclidean, cosine, inner-product, and filtered queries exactly under updates. On four H100 GPUs, it answers 10,000 exact queries over one billion vectors in 1.1 seconds instead of five minutes. On eleven open LLMs, it retrieves the exact top-10 attention keys 2.2x to 13.1x faster than exhaustive search. In sparse attention over one million tokens, it runs 3.1x faster than bf16 selection with FlashInfer, which misses the exact top-64 for most queries.
papers.summary: Zarc: exact k-NN (Euclidean, cosine, inner product, filtered, with updates) over a billion vectors on 4 H100s, keeping only the short rows of half-precision pruning proofs on GPU and fetching remaining candidates from host memory; 10k exact queries in 1.1 s vs 5 min, and 2.2-13.1x faster exact top-10 attention-key retrieval.

papers.title: SJG: A Skyline Joint Graph for Multi-Component Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search
papers.abstract: Graph-based indexes enable efficient approximate nearest neighbor search at scale by linking similar objects. In applications such as product retrieval and rental listing search, similarity depends on several components whose relative importance varies across queries. The challenge is that the index must select neighbors during construction, but the query weights that determine which objects are closest are not yet known. A straightforward approach is to index each component separately. However, merging the results of these searches can miss the nearest neighbor under the weighted distance. A joint graph allows a search to follow links across components, helping to avoid such misses, but selecting neighbors separately within each component can leave redundant edges, and keeping component hierarchies synchronized limits parallel construction. To address these limitations, we propose the Skyline Joint Graph (SJG). Although query weights can change the ranking of candidate neighbors, the dominance relation among them is independent of those weights. SJG exploits this property by pooling candidates across components and retaining the Skyline for each node, thereby enabling efficient approximate nearest neighbor search under different query weights while supporting parallel graph construction. Extensive experiments on six real-world datasets demonstrate that SJG achieves up to $27.9\times$ the query throughput of baseline methods at 90% Recall@10, while accelerating single-threaded index construction by up to $201\times$. Its index requires at least 36% less space than the smallest baseline index.
papers.summary: Skyline Joint Graph for ANN under query-weighted multi-component distances: since dominance among candidates is weight-independent, each node keeps the skyline of candidates pooled across components; up to 27.9x throughput at 90% Recall@10 and much faster construction.

papers.title: PROSPER: LLMs as Sparse Retrievers for First-Stage Product Search
papers.abstract: Product search is a crucial component of large-scale e-commerce platforms, where first-stage retrieval should achieve high recall while ensuring efficient online deployment. Sparse retrieval remains attractive for this setting due to its interpretability and deployability, yet it suffers from severe vocabulary mismatch challenges, especially for short queries and product titles. Large language models (LLMs) offer strong semantic capabilities, but directly applying them to sparse retrieval in product search introduces new challenges: (i) semantic expansion may distort critical literal signals such as brand names and model identifiers; and (ii) learning meaningful sparse representations is difficult in the high-dimensional vocabulary space induced by LLMs.To address these challenges, we propose PROSPER, a framework that uses LLMs as sparse retrievers for product search while explicitly preserving lexical fidelity. PROSPER combines (i) a literal residual network that alleviates lexical expansion hallucination by reinforcing underweighted literal terms through a residual compensation mechanism; and (ii) a lexical focusing window that uses top-k selection for rapid early sparsification and effective training initialization. Extensive offline evaluations and large-scale online A/B tests demonstrate that PROSPER consistently improves over existing sparse retrievers, and provides revenue gains for industrial hybrid retrieval systems.
papers.summary: PROSPER uses LLMs as learned sparse retrievers for first-stage product search, with a literal residual network that re-weights under-weighted literal terms (brands, model ids) and a top-k lexical focusing window for early sparsification; offline gains and online A/B revenue gains.

papers.title: Pixel as the Common Language: Unified Multimodal Embedding via Visual Rendering
papers.abstract: Multimodal embedding models map heterogeneous inputs into a shared representation space, yet text-only, image-only, and composed inputs are still presented in distinct formats and follow different routes through the model. This fragmentation prevents heterogeneous tasks from jointly optimizing the same end-to-end encoding process, limiting supervision transfer across input configurations. To address this issue, we propose unification before encoding and instantiate this paradigm in RenderEmbed. The framework uses Visual Substrate Rendering to convert heterogeneous inputs into a common visual substrate for encoding with a VLM. From the resulting visual tokens, Progressive Hierarchical Anchor Encoding produces compact retrieval representations by interleaving learnable anchors and fusing their states across layers, retaining broad context and fine-grained cues. Interventional Rendering Learning trains these representations to remain sensitive to content changes and stable across rendering variations through complementary semantic and rendering interventions. Extensive experiments on MMEB and ViDoRe v2, spanning diverse retrieval tasks, show that RenderEmbed outperforms prior state-of-the-art models at the same scale and exhibits strong out-of-domain generalization. Compared with MetaEmbed, RenderEmbed improves MMEB Overall Precision@1 by 1.7 points, with a larger 2.1-point gain on out-of-domain tasks. Transfer and scaling analyses further show that a shared visual pathway enables more effective learning from heterogeneous supervision.
papers.summary: RenderEmbed renders text, image and composed inputs into one visual substrate before encoding with a VLM, with anchor tokens for compact embeddings; beats same-size SOTA on MMEB and ViDoRe v2 (+1.7 P@1 over MetaEmbed).

papers.title: Ask Again: Answer-List Instability in Generative Engines
papers.abstract: Visibility in generative search engines is measured by which entities appear in responses, and in what order. Ask an engine the same question twice and the answer list can change: a different ordering, or different items altogether. Across 60,000 responses, we find that answers to the same prompt name a different first item 32% of the time, and even two answers with the same items disagree on which comes first. The first position is a measurement target of its own. A "clear leader" emerges after seven or eight runs, which are the budgets recommended for brand and source monitoring, but a "close leader" only about half the time. After 25 runs, a close leader is identified only 60% of the time. Variability between engines is larger than within the same engine. For open-ended prompts, the gap is more than double that for determinate ones. Search queries and cited sites observed leave most of the disagreement unexplained. Visibility measurement should report, for each engine, which items appear and how often each comes first, each with its own quantification of uncertainty.
papers.summary: Over 60,000 responses, generative search engines name a different first item 32% of the time for the same prompt; a close leader is identified only 60% of the time after 25 runs. Visibility metrics should report per-item appearance and first-position frequencies with uncertainty.

papers.title: Make Position Uninformative: Exchangeable Self-Distillation Flattens the Lost-in-the-Middle Curve
papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented language models answer well when the relevant document comes first or last and poorly when it sits in the middle. Some fine-tuning recipes lift the middle by lowering the start. We show how training contexts teach positional bias. With a uniform answer slot and shuffled distractors, the optimal reader ignores position. Building on this result, Exchangeable Self-Distillation (ExSD) trains a small adapter on shuffled contexts to reproduce the model's answer when it reads the answer document alone. It needs no gold answers and only a few thousand examples. On six models from 1.5B to 32B parameters, ExSD raises both average and worst-position accuracy against the frozen model, including on a held-out test split. In controlled LoRA comparisons, it significantly improves both criteria over Pos2Distill. Against CORD, mean differences are not significant, while worst-position accuracy improves significantly in the 20- and 30-document settings. ExSD also matches or beats gold-answer fine-tuning, changes behavior on other tasks far less, and transfers to unseen tasks. Head probes show greater reliance on content over position.
papers.summary: Shows that with a uniform answer slot and shuffled distractors the optimal reader ignores position, and trains an adapter (ExSD) on shuffled contexts to match the model's answer given the gold document alone; flattens the lost-in-the-middle curve on 1.5B-32B models without gold answers.

papers.title: S$^2$LMR: Supervised Sequential Long-Context Multi-Step Retriever
papers.abstract: Multi-step retrieval over long contexts is a key capability for retrieval-augmented generation, but strong existing approaches are costly and complex to train. Supervised retrievers are far simpler and cheaper, yet they fall well behind in this setting. We show that this gap stems not from supervised training itself, but from three misalignments between training and inference: easy training negatives, noisy retrieval prefixes, and position-agnostic scoring. Guided by this analysis, we introduce S$^2$LMR, a simple yet effective supervised sequential retriever that models multi-step retrieval as the evolution of an explicit textual state encoded by a single shared Transformer. On long-context reasoning, multi-hop QA, and needle-in-a-haystack benchmarks with context lengths ranging from 4K to 10M tokens, S$^2$LMR achieves performance comparable to state-of-the-art methods, substantially outperforming prior supervised retrievers. Notably, it requires only $\sim$2 hours of training on a single A6000 for contexts of up to 10M tokens, while remaining robust across a wide range of hyperparameter settings.
papers.summary: S²LMR, a supervised sequential multi-step retriever over long contexts (4K-10M tokens) that fixes three train/inference mismatches (easy negatives, noisy prefixes, position-agnostic scoring); matches costlier methods with ~2 GPU-hours of training.
